mcqs.question: A test suite's runtime grows from 2 minutes to 35 minutes over a year as the codebase grows. What is the most significant practical consequence beyond the extra CI cost?
options: None — as long as the suite still passes, runtime has no effect on engineering behavior
Engineers stop waiting for the run, push and context-switch, and a failure now costs an interruption and lost context instead of an immediate correction
The suite automatically becomes less accurate at longer runtimes
Longer runtimes always indicate a bug in the test framework itself
mcqs.explanation: Suite runtime shapes behavior directly — under a couple minutes people wait and fix immediately, but past a certain point they push and move on, so a failure costs a context-switch and reload instead of a quick correction. Runtime doesn't affect test accuracy or imply a framework bug; the cost is behavioral, not technical.

mcqs.question: A team shards its test suite across 10 CI workers by splitting test files evenly by count, but one shard consistently takes 4x longer than the others. What's the most likely cause?
options: That worker machine has a hardware defect
Splitting by file count ignores actual runtime — a shard containing a few slow integration-heavy files can take far longer than shards of many fast unit test files
Sharding by file count is impossible; only sharding by directory works
The test suite has a shared-state bug causing cascading failures
mcqs.explanation: An even split by test count doesn't guarantee an even split by runtime — a shard that happens to contain a few slow integration tests can dominate total time even with fewer files. The fix is sharding by historical per-test runtime, not by count; this isn't a hardware or shared-state issue.

mcqs.question: A team enables auto-retry so any failed test reruns twice before being reported as failed. What's the risk of relying on this as the primary flakiness strategy?
options: Auto-retry has no downside — it only affects genuinely environmental flakiness
Auto-retry makes the suite run slower with no benefit
It can paper over a real, intermittent bug by making the suite appear green even when a genuine defect fails some fraction of the time
Auto-retry is only usable for e2e tests, never for unit tests
mcqs.explanation: Auto-retry is useful for genuinely transient causes like a network blip, but used as the sole strategy it can silently absorb a real intermittent bug into a passing build, hiding a defect rather than fixing it. It does add some runtime cost on retries, and it isn't restricted to any particular test layer.

mcqs.question: A test in code that's actively being modified right now starts flaking. Which response fits best, compared to quarantining it indefinitely?
options: Delete the test immediately to unblock the team
Quarantine it permanently since it's flaky
Block merges until it's fixed, since the flake is tied to code currently under active work and fixing it now is cheap and high-context
Ignore it since flakiness is expected at scale
mcqs.explanation: A newly-introduced flake in code someone is actively working on is the case where blocking until fixed makes sense — the context is fresh and the fix is cheap right now, unlike a long-standing flake in stable code. Deleting throws away real coverage, and quarantining forever or ignoring it both defer a cheap fix into a future, more expensive one.

mcqs.question: A team needs test data that reflects the messy distributions of real production data (unusual formatting, edge-case values) for load and edge-case testing, but can't use raw production data directly. What's the appropriate approach?
options: Hand-write additional edge cases into existing fixture files
Use anonymized production snapshots — real data with identifying information stripped or hashed — to preserve realistic distributions without exposing real user data
Use only synthetic data, since it always reproduces real-world messiness accurately
Skip this kind of testing since production data can never be used for tests
mcqs.explanation: Anonymized snapshots preserve the real-world messiness synthetic generation often misses, while stripping the identifying information that makes raw production data unusable for privacy/compliance reasons. Synthetic data doesn't reliably reproduce real distributions, hand-written fixtures don't scale to genuine variety, and production data being off-limits in raw form doesn't mean the need for realistic data disappears.

mcqs.question: In a microservices architecture with 30 services, why does a shared contract broker scale better than broad integration tests that spin up every real service?
options: It turns an O(services²) verification problem into roughly O(services), since each service verifies its own published contracts independently rather than every pair being tested live together
The broker eliminates the need for any testing between services entirely
It works only because all 30 services happen to share one database
Broad integration tests and contract testing catch entirely unrelated categories of bugs, so the comparison doesn't apply
mcqs.explanation: Without a broker, verifying every consumer-provider pair live scales quadratically with service count; with a broker, each provider checks its contracts against all recorded consumer expectations without any of those consumers running live, making it linear. It doesn't remove the need for any inter-service testing, doesn't depend on shared database infrastructure, and both approaches target largely the same integration-shape bugs.
